highlights:
### We tell you when we cancel a price increase

You say to your agent

> “Is the H100 price increase that you announced still on?”

If we cancel a price increase that we announced, the dashboard shows a notice that says so. Each organization that got the email about the increase gets a second email that cancels it. The email includes the text of the first one. See Rates.

## October 14, 2026

1. 23:00 UTC

### Sandbox price increases come with notice too

You say to your agent

> “Will sandbox prices go up while my rollouts run?”

A sandbox rate increase now also comes at least 24 hours before it takes effect, and we tell you about it. That is any higher rate: active sandboxes, parked sandboxes and snapshots, or cold snapshots.

The dashboard shows a notice until a few days after the increase takes effect. The admins and billing members of each organization that used sandboxes in the last 90 days get an email. A new rate applies to each billing hour that starts at or after that time. See Rates.
2. 22:35 UTC

...

## October 13, 2026

1. 20:00 UTC

### We tell you about a price increase before it takes effect

You say to your agent

> “Is the price of an H100 going to change soon?”

A price increase now always comes at least 24 hours before it takes effect, and we tell you about it. An increase is a higher list price, or a smaller Friday, weekend, or batch job discount.

When we schedule an increase, the dashboard shows a notice until a few days after it takes effect. The admins and billing members of each organization that used that type in the last 90 days get an email.

Your agent sees it too. Until the increase takes effect, `create_node` and `get_node` carry it in `rate.upcoming_increase`, and `submit_job` carries it in `upcoming_increase`. The field gives the time it takes effect, the new list rate per GPU and per node, and the new discounts. A running node also gets a `price_change` event on `/v1/events`. See Rates.

...

If your image keeps files in its user's home directory, set `home` to a path that the image does not use. `get_node` now names the image files that the disk hides. The docs show the rules.

## October 8, 2026

1. 07:00 UTC

### The H100 price is now $5.04 per GPU-hour

On October 8 at 00:00 Pacific time, the H100 list price changed from $3.96 to $5.04 per GPU-hour. Per GPU-minute, the price changed from $0.066 to $0.084. A whole 8-GPU node now costs $40.32 per hour.

The new price applies to each minute that we bill from that time. This includes the minutes of nodes and jobs that were already running. Minutes before that time bill at the old price.

The discounts did not change, and they now apply to the new list price. Friday hours are 33% off, and Saturday and Sunday hours are 20% off, on the Pacific calendar. Batch jobs are 25% off the list price. The docs show the rates.

We did not tell you about this change before it took effect. We are sorry for the late notice. If you have a question about your bill, send it to us on the contact page.

results.author: Mercatus Compute
highlights:
General Sep 15, 2026 8 min read

H100 rents for $3.84 an hour on average, H200 for $4.43, B200 for $6.39, with a 4x to 6x spread between the cheapest and most expensive provider on each. Current hourly rates by provider from the Mercatus GPU Index, what an 8-GPU node costs per month, and how the hourly rate sets the floor under token prices.

...

An NVIDIA H100 rents for $3.84 per GPU-hour on average across 27 cloud providers, an H200 for $4.43 across 20, and a B200 for $6.39 across 12, as tracked by the Mercatus GPU Index on September 13, 2026. Those averages hide the number that actually matters to a buyer: the same H100 lists at $1.79 an hour from one provider and $10.00 from another. On an 8-GPU node running around the clock, that is the difference between $10,500 and $58,400 a month for identical hardware.

This page is the static reference for that market: the current average and range for each data-center GPU, the hourly rate at every provider the index tracks for H100, H200, and B200, what a node costs per month at each end of the range, and how a GPU-hour translates into the price of a token. The live version, updated every five minutes, is the Mercatus GPU Index.

results.title: The same GPU, at very different prices · infratoapp
highlights:
The median gap between the cheapest and dearest seller of an identical card is 3.8×. The widest is the V100-16GB: $0.24 per GPU-hour at Verda (DataCrunch) against $2.85 at Runcrate, a gap of 11.8×. An H100 SXM 80GB — the card most of this market is actually built on — runs from $2.16 to $6.16 across 13 sellers, a gap of 2.8×.

These are headline on-demand rates, before any commitment discount, for the same part. Not a similar part, not a different memory configuration, and not one region against another.

results.title: Flopper Now Tracks GPU Rental Prices Across 24 Cloud Providers | Flopper.io
highlights:
337 per-GPU hourly rates from 24 clouds, refreshed every six hours, with price history back to July 2026. The spec database now tells you what each accelerator costs to rent, and who is cheapest today.

Published September 9, 2026 · Flopper.io Research

Flopper.io started as a specification database: peak TFLOPS by precision, memory, bandwidth and power for every datacenter GPU. Specs answer half of the buying question. The other half is price, and that number lives on 24 different pricing pages, in 24 different units. As of today, the pricing index collects 337 live listings from 24 GPU cloud providers, covering 89 GPUs, normalized to one unit: US dollars per GPU per hour. The pipeline refreshes every six hours and has recorded every price change since 14 July 2026, so each GPU page now carries a price history alongside its spec sheet.

## What the Same GPU Costs, Cloud to Cloud

The spread is the story. On the day of publication, an on-demand H100 SXM5 80 GB (2022) is listed by 16 providers, and the most expensive listing costs nearly seven times the cheapest. The B200 (2024) shows the same pattern with a three-fold gap across eight clouds. Some of that gap is real: interconnect, storage, support and region all cost money. Some of it is simply price discovery that has not happened yet, because nobody was lining the numbers up.

| GPU | Providers | Cheapest on-demand | Highest on-demand |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| NVIDIA H100 SXM5 80 GB | 16 | $1.79/hr | $12.29/hr |
| NVIDIA A100 SXM4 80 GB | 11 | $1.40/hr | $4.10/hr |
| NVIDIA L40S 48 GB | 11 | $0.87/hr | $2.25/hr |
| NVIDIA H200 SXM 141 GB | 10 | $2.99/hr | $10.60/hr |
| NVIDIA B200 SXM 180 GB | 8 | $4.09/hr | $14.00/hr |
| NVIDIA B300 SXM 288 GB | 6 | $7.40/hr | $11.19/hr |
| AMD Instinct MI300X 192 GB | 5 | $2.39/hr | $6.00/hr |

On-demand, per-GPU, USD, as recorded on 9 September 2026. Spot, community and reserved listings are excluded from the range. Each GPU links to its live pricing page, which will have moved on by the time you read this.

...

- Per GPU, per hour, in USD. Node prices are divided by the GPU count. Monthly rates are divided by 730 hours. Non-USD prices are converted at the live exchange rate on the day of the sync.
- Pricing types are kept apart. On-demand (191 listings), spot or preemptible (31), marketplace community hosts (111) and reserved commitments (4) never share a row. The headline cheapest price on each GPU page is always on-demand, so an interruptible instance cannot masquerade as the market rate.
- Every listing maps to one canonical part. A provider's "H100" is matched to the exact variant it sells, SXM5 or PCIe, 80 GB or 94 GB, so a PCIe price never dilutes the SXM figure. Names the matcher cannot place are logged and dropped rather than guessed.
- Bad data is quarantined, not published. A listing that lands far outside its GPU's price band is held back and flagged for review. Median, dispersion and FP8-per-dollar figures on the pricing index are calculated so that a single bad listing cannot move them.

...

A price comparison that only shows today cannot tell you whether $2.99 for an H200 is a bargain or the new normal. Since 14 July 2026 the pipeline has recorded 2,297 price points across 58 days and 101 GPUs, appending a row every time a listing changes. Each GPU pricing page plots the last 30 days with one line per provider, so you can see who cut, who held, and who quietly raised.

The index also reports a 30-day change per GPU. That figure compares the same providers' listings at both ends of the window, so a new cloud joining coverage registers as more data, not as a price move.

results.title: Why H100 Rental Prices Rose 40% While Token Prices Fell
results.author: Framesta Fernando
highlights:
> TL;DR: H100 rental prices rose almost 40% between October 2025 and March 2026, from $1.70 to $2.35 per GPU-hour on one-year contracts, while API token prices kept falling. The cost floor under inference is rising even as the sticker price above it drops, and every self-hosting business case written before that shift is now wrong.

...

The number worth reading is the rental contract. H100 one-year rental pricing rose from a low of $1.70 per GPU-hour in October 2025 to $2.35 by March 2026, close to 40%, and on-demand capacity was described as sold out across all GPU types, with half the providers surveyed unable to quote even 8 nodes of H100s or H200s (SemiAnalysis's H100 rental price index). That is not a market pricing in abundance. That is a market rationing.

...

### Q: How much does an H100 cost to rent per hour?

Published index pricing for one-year H100 contracts was $2.35 per GPU-hour as of March 2026, up from a $1.70 low in October 2025. On-demand and short-term rates sit higher and vary widely by provider and region, and during the 2026 crunch several providers could not quote capacity at any advertised rate. Treat a quoted rate as valid only for the term you can actually sign.
